synopsis: The CMS is being developed as a successor to proximity warning: it automatically brakes when the operator does not react, and adding braking changes the safety-engineering scope rather than merely the performance metric [f1, f2955, f5221]. Prototype hardware and software are due in mid-2027, with validation required in under four months afterward—a substantial compression relative to the three-to-four-year validation history reported for comparable functions [f2, f3, f4, f4391]. Requirements span more than 100 job-site types, more than 10 operating scenarios per machine, multiple machine models, and weather and lighting conditions including rain, snow, fog, dust, dusk, darkness and glare [f5130, f2956, f285]. This broad scope is in tension with the glossary's expected reverse-only, low-speed wheel-loader operating domain and the recommendation to test forward, reverse, start-from-rest, turning and swing separately [f11397, f2996]. Evidence remains limited: independent off-road collision-system field data are old and sparse, underground injury figures lack speed and motion detail needed for braking design, and braking depends on sensor detection [f5169, f3256, f11302]. The recommended programme architecture combines systems-engineering V&V and TEMP-style test planning with evidence-based stage gates, reserving TRLs for critical-technology maturity [f9588, f9589, f9590].
